sentences.text: "Ownership" is a word the industry's been quietly hollowing out for years, and I'd argue most of us haven't noticed because the hole keeps getting bigger one firmware update at a time.

claims.claim: The technology industry has been hollowing out the meaning of ownership for years.
Firmware updates are the incremental mechanism by which this hollowing out occurs.

sentences.text: When you buy a device and the maker can reach back in and disable features after the sale, you don't own that device – you've leased it.
You've purchased a conditional license to use it, at the manufacturer's ongoing pleasure, until you haven't.
Think about what it meant to buy a physical object before everything got a software layer.
The seller hands it over, the transaction closes, and their claim on it ends: that's what a sale is.
The dealer doesn't get to send a signal six months later that disables your heated seats because they've launched a subscription tier for climate control.
If they tried that (and we all know they'd love to), we'd call it fraud, and we'd be right.

claims.claim: Manufacturers desire or would prefer to disable hardware features and monetise them as subscriptions.

sentences.text: But that's exactly the architecture that device makers have been quietly building into products for a decade, and because the mechanism is invisible – a patch that downloads at 3am while you're asleep – the outrage hasn't kept pace with reality.

claims.claim: Device makers have been building into products the architecture of post-sale remote feature modification for roughly a decade.
Such modifications are delivered invisibly via patches that download while users sleep.
Public outrage over this practice has not kept pace with its actual prevalence.

sentences.text: Here's what's actually happening to your stuff.
You pay full retail, take the thing home, and use it for a year, maybe two.
Then the company decides the feature you factored into your purchase decision is now a premium add-on, and it vanishes from your unit in a silent update.

claims.claim: Companies have reclassified previously included device features as premium add-ons and removed them via silent software updates after purchase.

sentences.text: And if you find out at all, it's in a change-log written for lawyers, not users.

claims.claim: Manufacturers disclose feature changes in changelogs written in legalistic language not intended to be read by ordinary users.

sentences.text: What would you call that if it happened to a refrigerator?
You'd call it fraud, and you'd want the attorney general involved.
But because it's software, we've somehow agreed to treat it as a terms-of-service question rather than a property question, which is exactly where the industry needs us to be.

claims.claim: Society and legal institutions currently treat post-sale software feature removal as a terms-of-service matter rather than a property matter.
The technology industry has an interest in maintaining this framing and has worked toward it.

sentences.text: John Deere has made the underlying logic explicit: the software running your tractor is licensed, not sold, so the company retains ongoing control over what you do with the machine you nominally own.

claims.claim: John Deere has taken the position that its tractor software is licensed rather than sold, giving the company ongoing control over customer use of the hardware.

sentences.text: Tesla has remotely modified battery range on vehicles that customers already paid for.

claims.claim: Tesla remotely modified battery range on vehicles that customers had already purchased.

sentences.text: I think these aren't outliers; they're the model the whole industry is working toward.
The physical object transfers; the functional capability stays on a leash the manufacturer holds.
The "it's in the EULA" defense is where this gets genuinely dishonest.
Yes, technically there's a clause (buried past forty screens of boilerplate, in type sized for discouragement rather than reading) that discloses some version of the arrangement.

claims.claim: EULAs typically bury relevant clauses deep in lengthy boilerplate text presented in small or discouraging type.

sentences.text: What kind of consent gets manufactured that way?
That's not consent – it's a legal fig leaf, and we shouldn't let the industry use it to pull this shit with a straight face.
A transaction where the seller retains ongoing unilateral control over the product's functionality is not a sale.
It's a rental with a one-time upfront fee, and calling it a purchase is a lie.
I don't think this is hard to fix, in principle.
We need mandatory disclosure at point of sale for any feature subject to post-purchase modification – not tucked in the EULA, but on the box, in plain language.
We need right-to-repair statutes with real teeth that don't carve out the software layer (where all the control actually lives).

claims.claim: Existing right-to-repair statutes carve out or otherwise fail to cover the software layer of devices.
The software layer is where manufacturers' actual control over device functionality resides.

sentences.text: And we need courts (I know, I know) to stop treating 6,000-word boilerplate agreements as evidence of informed consent.

claims.claim: Courts currently treat lengthy boilerplate EULA agreements as sufficient evidence of informed consent.

sentences.text: The word "sale" should mean something.
Until legislatures decide it does, every "buy" button is a promise the seller never intends to keep.

claims.claim: Sellers of software-governed devices do not genuinely intend to honor the implicit promise of full ownership conveyed by a purchase transaction.
